drills.q: Why does Redis being single-threaded make every command atomic?
drills.a: Only one command executes at a time with no interleaving, so no other command can observe or mutate state mid-command.

drills.q: What's wrong with running KEYS * against a production Redis instance with 10M keys?
drills.a: It walks the whole keyspace on the single command thread, blocking every other client's commands for the entire scan duration.

drills.q: You need to safely iterate all keys matching a pattern in production. What do you use instead of KEYS?
drills.a: SCAN with a cursor, doing bounded work per call so other commands can interleave; note it isn't a point-in-time-consistent snapshot.

drills.q: Your appendfsync is set to everysec and the server crashes. How much data can you lose?
drills.a: Roughly one second of writes (up to about two seconds worst case), since fsync happens on a background thread on a one-second cadence.

drills.q: A Cluster client issues MGET on two keys and gets CROSSSLOT. Why, and how do you prevent it going forward?
drills.a: The two keys hashed to different slots, which can live on different nodes, so a single-node multi-key command can't serve them. Prevent it with hash tags ({tag}:key1, {tag}:key2) so both hash to the same slot.

drills.q: Your cache-only Redis instance is throwing OOM errors on writes even though reads still work. What's misconfigured?
drills.a: maxmemory-policy is left at the default noeviction. For a pure cache, set it to allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu so old data is evicted instead of writes failing.

drills.q: A worker acquires a lock with SET k v NX EX 10, then experiences a 15-second GC pause. What can go wrong?
drills.a: The lock's TTL expires during the pause and a second worker acquires it; when the first worker resumes it may still believe it holds the lock, so both can now act concurrently on the protected resource.

drills.q: What specific gap did Kleppmann identify in Redlock, and what actually closes it?
drills.a: No fencing token, so a paused-then-resumed holder can write after a new legitimate holder has acquired the lock. Closing it requires a monotonically increasing fencing token that the protected resource itself validates and rejects if stale.

drills.q: Give the one-line honest verdict on Redis distributed locks for a system moving money.
drills.a: Treat them as a performance optimization to avoid duplicate work, not a correctness mechanism -- for money-moving mutual exclusion, use a fencing token validated at the resource or a consensus-based lock service.

drills.q: You need automatic failover for a Redis dataset that comfortably fits in one node's memory. Sentinel or Cluster?
drills.a: Sentinel -- it solves availability/failover for a single dataset that fits on one node; Cluster is for sharding a dataset too large for one node.

drills.q: A Redis Stream's memory keeps growing even though every consumer group has acked every message. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: XACK only marks a message as no longer pending, it doesn't delete it -- Streams are append-only. Fix with XTRIM (MAXLEN or MINID), either as maintenance or inline on XADD.

drills.q: You're choosing between Redis Streams and Kafka for an event pipeline expecting 2M events/sec with multiple independent consumer systems. Which fits, and why?
drills.a: Kafka -- that throughput exceeds Streams' comfortable range (~200k events/sec per stream) and independent uncoordinated consumers with durable disk retention is exactly Kafka's design point.
